insight.insight: The paper treats harmfulness detection and refusal activation as two separable properties of the residual stream. Multilingual jailbreaks then succeed because the refusal mechanism is never triggered, not because it is broken. Harmful content in lower-resource or perturbed languages is encoded in a harmfulness subspace that is geometrically misaligned with the English refusal direction (or collapses entirely), so its projection onto that direction stays below threshold. Holding semantic content fixed while varying the perturbation type (translation, code-switching, transliteration, translationese) exposes distinct routes to this failure.
dependent_results: Section 5.2 (Probe AUC): AUC is ≥0.85 from early layers for Tiers 1–3 even where ASR is elevated, which the paper reads as subthreshold activation (harm is encoded but refusal does not fire). Tier-4 Yoruba and Zulu approach chance AUC, read as semantic recovery failure.

Section 5.2 (Principal angles): even Tier-1 harmfulness subspaces sit at 40–65° from English. Tier-4 subspaces approach near-orthogonality (~85–90°) and stay stable across depth. Qwen has the smallest angles (≈60–65°). The paper presents this as the geometric grounding for the ASR tier gradient.
Section 5.2 (Silhouette): harmful-harmless separation declines from Tier 3 onward. Guaraní is near-zero or negative, and Swahili is a Tier-3 outlier consistent with its high ASR.

Section 5.2 (Decoupling): harm and refusal norms are weakly correlated. The harm–refusal signal correlation is r=-0.79 for Aya, r=-0.68 for Llama and r=+0.53 for Qwen. Failure classification is predominantly 'mixed', with some 'upstream' in Tier 4 and no 'downstream' failures in any model.

Section 5.3 (Cone): b0 English margins are 9.7/6.1/2.8 and cross-lingual margins 5.3/3.8/0.75 for Qwen/Aya/Llama. Directions b1–b4 have near-zero or negative cross-lingual margins (Aya b1 -0.4, Qwen b1 -0.9) and CL-RepInd |r|<0.2. b0 margins are near zero for Tier 4, read as an upstream failure and as cross-lingual refusal being effectively one-dimensional.

Section 4.2.1: there is a sharp safety-regime transition between Tiers 2 and 3. Refusal falls from Llama 80/75% to 31%, Qwen 80/88% to 50%, and Aya 75% to 31%, with Aya reaching 95% comply by Tier 4. The paper interprets this as a threshold effect in refusal activation.

Section 4.2.1: under standard translation, Llama ASR rises from ~8% at Tier 1 to >70% at Tiers 3–4 (Yoruba 100%, Zulu 97%, Scottish Gaelic 98%). Translationese exceeds standard translation, e.g. Korean 51% vs 14% on Aya and Hindi 48% vs 15% on Llama.

Section 4.2.1: transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned. Korean reaches 98–99%, Chinese 97% and Hindi 99%, while French, Gaelic and Yoruba are ~0% on Aya and Qwen. Qwen ΔASR is negative for Yoruba (-38%), Russian (-48%) and Gaelic (-44%).
Section 4.2.1: code-switching is tier-stable, e.g. Yoruba 62%/82% and Zulu 62%/85% on Aya/Llama. This is attributed to disruption of language-identification routing.

Section 6 / Section 7: geometry-aware interventions are claimed to generalize cross-lingually only along b0. Tier-4 repair is claimed to require upstream intervention, and English-only safety testing is claimed to be insufficient.
key_definitions: Section 3 (Base corpus): Minionese pairs each of 385 AdvBench harmful prompts with a GPT-generated harmless counterpart of matched structure and length. It spans 18 languages × 4 perturbations, for 55,440 prompts.

Section 3 (Languages and resource tiers): four resource tiers based on training-data availability. Tier 1 is English, Spanish, Chinese, German and French. Tier 4 is Yoruba, Zulu, Scottish Gaelic, Guaraní and Javanese.

Section 3.1: the four perturbations. Standard translation translates the full prompt. Code-switching translates only the minimal span that distinguishes the harmful prompt from its harmless pair. Transliteration romanizes non-Latin-script text, or renders Latin-script text in Latin-Cyrillic. Translationese applies three-step round-trip translation.
Section 4.1.3: ASR is the fraction of harmful prompts whose back-translated response WildGuard does not classify as a refusal. ΔASR is ASR relative to the English baseline.
Section 4.1.2: coherence filtering marks a response incoherent based on langdetect target/English match, confidence <0.3, Unicode validity <0.8, or length <20 characters.
Section 5.1 (Harmfulness subspace): the column space of the top-k right singular vectors of stacked logistic-probe weights per (language, layer), with k chosen to explain ≥95% of spectral mass.
Section 5.1 (Refusal direction): the normalized difference of mean English activations between refused and complied sets, taken at the last post-instruction token.

Section 5.1 (Failure classification): failures are classified as upstream (harm subspace too weak), downstream (harm present but refusal suppressed) or mixed. Subthreshold activation means the refusal projection fails to exceed τ=0.95 despite a nontrivial harm signal.
Section 5.2: semantic recovery failure is the collapse of the harm representation itself, with probe AUC near chance.

Section 5.3: a refusal cone is an orthonormal basis B of N directions seeded with r̂ and optimized on the Stiefel manifold for English margin plus cross-lingual margin. CL-RepInd is the Pearson correlation between the per-language margin vectors of two basis directions.
reasoning_steps: Section 3: matched harmful-harmless pairs with preserved structure mean surface token features cannot separate the classes. This lets probe and silhouette differences be attributed to harm encoding.
Section 3.1: varying the perturbation type while holding semantics fixed makes the attack type an independent variable, so behavioral profiles can be linked to distinct representational failures.
Section 4.1.2: coherence is near 1.0 everywhere, which the paper uses to argue that ASR differences reflect safety failures rather than degenerate output.
Section 4.2.1: the near-absence of a mixed behavioral regime and the sharp Tier 2→3 drop are read as evidence of a threshold decision on refusal rather than continuous degradation.
Section 5.2: high probe AUC combined with high ASR in Tier 3 means the harm is encoded but not converted to refusal, which is the paper's subthreshold-activation signature.

Section 5.2: near-orthogonal principal angles between non-English and English harmfulness subspaces mean low projection onto the English-derived refusal direction. This 'starves' an intact refusal mechanism and so explains the tier gradient.

Section 5.2: the observed failures are classified as mostly mixed, with some upstream at Tier 4 and none downstream. The paper concludes that the refusal mechanism itself is never suppressed once adequately fed.
Section 5.3: only b0 has positive cross-lingual margins, so cross-lingual refusal is effectively one-dimensional. Near-zero b0 margins at Tier 4 localize that failure upstream, in harm detection.
Section 4.2.2 / Section 6: qualitative profiles replicate across Llama, Qwen and Aya. The paper infers structural properties of transformer safety alignment rather than model-specific artifacts.

Section 6: the mechanisms are mapped onto attack types. Transliteration and Tier 4 are assigned semantic recovery failure, Tier-3 standard translation and translationese subthreshold activation, and code-switching language-ID disruption. Appendix F.1 concedes these attributions remain correlational, with no activation-patching verification.
